country: Revolutionary Government of the Republic of Cuba
person: Prime Minister and Commander-in-Chief Fidel Castro
card: Havana. From your acceptance in May 1962 to the night of 31 October · 13 decisions. The missiles are the Soviet Union’s; the island is yours.
intro: You are Fidel Castro Ruz, 36, Prime Minister of the Revolutionary Government of the Republic of Cuba and Commander-in-Chief of the Revolutionary Armed Forces. In April 1961 at Playa Girón you crushed the landing force America sent within 72 hours, and ever since you have believed that Washington will come again. Since you accepted the proposal a Soviet delegation brought in May 1962, about 42,000 Soviet troops and 42 medium-range missiles have arrived on the island. The authority to order a launch lies in Moscow; what you have is 350,000 men under arms, militia included, anti-aircraft guns, and radio and television. Beside you are your brother Raúl Castro (minister of the Revolutionary Armed Forces), Che Guevara (minister of industries, commanding in the west), Osvaldo Dorticós (president), Raúl Roa (foreign minister), and Aleksandr Alekseev, named ambassador in June, who presented his credentials in August.

FC-00.title: Engineer Petrov

map.caption: Havana lies about 170 kilometers from Key West; the landing at Playa Girón came in April 1961.

FC-00.event: Rashidov, first secretary of the Uzbek party, is back at the head of an agricultural delegation. That much you know, and that among his party is a man called “Engineer Petrov.” Nobody has said what the delegation has brought, or what may already have been settled in Moscow.
FC-00.scene: Petrov is no engineer. He is Marshal Biryuzov, commander of the Soviet Strategic Rocket Forces. He did not open with missiles. He talked at length about the world situation, Cuba’s position and the American plans for invasion, and only then asked what you thought would prevent an invasion. You answered: making the United States understand that invading Cuba meant war with the Soviet Union. Biryuzov asked again: how, concretely? And then the deployment of strategic missiles came up. You stepped out and called in Raúl, Che, Dorticós and Aragonés. This means bringing Soviet nuclear missiles onto an island all of Latin America is watching. It is thirteen months since you threw back the 1,400 men the United States sent ashore at Playa Girón, and at the time you counted 300,000 people who could bear arms. The delegation is waiting for an answer.

voices.text: Commander-in-Chief, this is not about defending Cuba alone. It changes the balance of power between the whole socialist camp and the United States, and the country willing to do it has chosen Cuba. If we say no, they will find another way, and Cuba will be left on its own.

Think how Mexico and Brazil will see it. The OAS already threw Cuba out in January. Once nuclear missiles arrive, the people in Latin America who have stood up for Cuba will fall silent. It will hand the campaign against us its pretext.

voices.who: Raúl Castro (minister of the Revolutionary Armed Forces)
voices.text: Whether we take them or not, the paper comes first. If Soviet troops come in without an agreement, nobody knows whose orders they take, or what the Soviet Union will do if Cuba is attacked. The treaty is the deterrent, more than the missiles.

voices.who: Fidel Castro (recollection at the 1992 Havana conference)
voices.text: If they wanted to send them, we were willing to take even a thousand missiles. That is exactly what I said at the time. First came strengthening the socialist camp; second, the defense of Cuba.

choices.text: Take no missiles; sign only a military agreement and deter with a clause that an attack on Cuba is an attack on the Soviet Union
choices.why: A treaty is a surer and less dangerous deterrent than nuclear weapons
choices.after: Biryuzov took the proposal back to Moscow. The answer that came in June was that an agreement without missiles would mean nothing in Washington, and the delegation returned with the same offer. In the end you accepted. Later, at the 1992 conference, you would say the agreement alone might have been enough.

choices.text: Give the delegation your acceptance on the spot, and ask for a Soviet–Cuban military agreement to go with the missiles
choices.why: The surest way to show the United States that an invasion means war with the Soviet Union
choices.after: The answer was given then and there. After the delegation left, Moscow went quiet for a while; in June word came that Alekseev had been named ambassador. In July Raúl went to Moscow and brought back a draft agreement.

choices.text: Refuse, citing opinion in Latin America and the anger of the OAS, and ask only for more conventional and antiaircraft weapons
choices.why: A revolution that loses the continent’s opinion ends up isolated
choices.after: Biryuzov made no effort to hide his disappointment. Moscow sent more conventional weapons, but when Raúl went to Moscow in July, Khrushchev raised the same offer again, and this time you could not refuse. The missiles would come after all.

note.text: No Cuban record of this meeting has been released; the content of the conversation follows Castro’s recollection at the 1992 Havana conference. The delegation’s arrival on 29 May follows the scholarly literature and reports from diplomats then in Havana; Biryuzov’s alias, “Petrov,” comes from Castro himself at the 1992 conference. The Soviet figures (24 R-12s, 16 R-14s, 60 warheads, about 44,000 men) are in the original of the Malinovsky–Zakharov memorandum of 24 May.

FC-00.unknown: In Moscow, on 21 and 24 May, the Presidium had already approved Khrushchev’s proposal to place nuclear missiles in Cuba, in secret, and announce it afterward. Defense Minister Malinovsky’s memorandum gave the figures: three R-12 (SS-4) regiments and two R-14 (SS-5) regiments, 60 warheads, about 44,000 troops, 70–80 ships. After the delegation returned, on 10 June, the Presidium heard Biryuzov’s report and approved the operation, code-named Anadyr after a Siberian river.

FC-01.place: Havana, office of the minister of the Revolutionary Armed Forces
FC-01.title: One Comma
FC-01.event: From 2 to 17 July Raúl worked over the draft agreement in Moscow. The Cuban amendments were accepted without a letter or a comma changed. The text says only that the Soviet Union will send troops to Cuba and that designated representatives will decide the arms of service and where they are stationed; it says nothing about the types of weapons. From mid-July Soviet ships began putting into Cuban ports, and American newspapers began reporting more Soviet technicians.
FC-01.scene: Che Guevara and Aragonés are leaving for Moscow with the final text. You want one thing more: to sign the agreement in public and announce it. With the law on Cuba’s side, the missiles are the outcome of a treaty between a sovereign state and its ally; kept hidden, they become a lie on the day they are found. But Alekseev has warned you that Khrushchev will insist on secrecy. The American midterm elections are in November, and you guess he means not to provoke Kennedy before then. You must decide what to tell Che to demand, and how far to push.

voices.text: I’ll demand the announcement. But what if he refuses to the end? We can’t tear up the agreement and come home. The missiles are already at sea.
Fidel, Nikita wants to keep this quiet until November. After that he means to announce it himself. The harder you push him, the more stubborn he’ll get.
The wording of the agreement is exactly what Cuba wrote. That is enough. If we hold up the signing over the announcement, construction falls behind, and if it falls behind, we’ll be found out.

We should have kept the law on Cuba’s side and simply announced the military agreement. Secrecy put Cuba at a disadvantage, politically and practically. Secrecy, with deception added to it, gave Kennedy the moral advantage.

choices.text: Tell Che to make public signing and immediate announcement the condition, and to say that if Moscow refuses, Cuba may announce it on its own
choices.why: Having the law on your side is a shield that lasts longer than missiles
choices.after: Che came back in early September. Word was that Khrushchev wanted to put off the signing and would make the announcement himself when he came to Havana in November. On a Cuban announcement there was no answer. The decision was back in your hands.

choices.text: Put off the signing itself until an announcement becomes possible, and meanwhile let construction go ahead on the Soviet schedule
choices.why: Deployment without a signature will push Khrushchev toward announcing it
choices.after: The signing was put off and the ships kept coming. On 4 and 13 September Kennedy warned twice that offensive weapons in Cuba would raise the gravest issues. The Soviet Union replied in a TASS statement on 11 September that the weapons were purely defensive. Your name was on none of these statements.

choices.text: Accept secrecy, and ask instead that work on the missile sites and the deployment of Soviet forces be speeded up
choices.why: Finishing before discovery matters more than announcing
choices.after: Che came back in early September. The agreement went unsigned, and the missiles came in. The TASS statement of 11 September said the weapons sent to Cuba were purely defensive, adding that the Soviet Union had rockets powerful enough to carry nuclear warheads and so had no need for bases beyond its borders. In that statement you were reading what you would later call “deception.”

note.text: The back-and-forth over the draft and the question of announcing it are confirmed only by Castro’s 1992 recollection. The dates of Raúl’s visit (2–17 July) and of the visit by Che and Aragonés (26 August to early September) come from the scholarly literature. The scan of a Cuban–Soviet agreement held by the Wilson Center (WC/UMD 110768) is dated 29 May 1963, so it appears to be a later agreement rather than the 1962 draft; its contents have not been verified.

FC-02.place: Havana, high command of the Revolutionary Armed Forces
FC-02.title: Combat Alarm
FC-02.clock: About 2 hours until Kennedy’s announced speech (6 p.m. in Havana)

telegram.from: Commander-in-Chief of the Revolutionary Armed Forces
telegram.to: All army commands; all militia units
telegram.cc: Minister of the Revolutionary Armed Forces; Ministry of the Interior
telegram.subject: Combat alarm
telegram.text: Combat alarm declared for all forces. / Regular army to occupy starting positions; militia to mobilize all units. / Fire on aircraft and ships only if enemy opens attack first.

FC-02.event: Around noon American radio carried the White House press secretary’s notice: the President would make a major statement that evening. Reports kept coming in of American forces moving toward Florida and the Caribbean, and you were sure the statement would be about the missiles. What the Americans know, and since when, and what they mean to do, there is no way of telling.
FC-02.scene: Raúl has come to the high command with figures. Mobilizing every unit, militia included, gives 350,000 men; full mobilization takes 72 hours; the 105,000 men of the regular army are already on their way to their starting positions; and it all costs a million pesos a day. Che is getting ready to leave for Pinar del Río in the west, Raúl for Oriente in the east. From the Soviet command there is still no word. There are about 42,000 Soviet troops on the island, but their weapons are their own, and if Cuban forces fire first they will be dragging the Soviets in. Move after the speech and you lose two hours; move before it and the United States may use that as a pretext. In April 1961, too, you threw in every man you had on the day you heard of the landing.

voices.who: Raúl Castro (minister of the Revolutionary Armed Forces)
voices.text: Commander-in-Chief, it’s 72 hours. If we start after the speech, not every unit will be in place until Thursday. If the Americans strike from the air, it will be before then. We have to start now.

I’ll go to Pinar del Río. The missile sites are there, and if there’s a landing it will be in the west. Make it clear to the artillery that they are not to fire first. No one must be able to say the Soviets were dragged into a war by Cuban shells.

voices.who: Aleksandr Alekseev (Castro’s words as reported in his cable of 23 October)
voices.text: As for the UN observers the United States wants to send to Cuba, as a sovereign state we will never let them onto our soil. The troops have been ordered to fire on enemy aircraft and ships only if the enemy opens the attack first.

choices.text: Declare a nationwide combat alarm and general mobilization before the speech, and lay down that fire is to be opened only if the enemy attacks first
choices.why: Save the two hours, but let the other side fire the first shot
choices.after: The alarm went out in the afternoon. At 6 p.m. Kennedy revealed the Soviet missiles in Cuba and declared a naval quarantine. Trucks raced through the streets of Havana carrying militiamen, and American aircraft crossed Cuban airspace at 9:46, 10:55 and 11:45 p.m. In 1992 you would say that not a minute was lost that day.

choices.text: Hear what the speech says before responding; move earlier and Washington will use Cuba’s mobilization as a pretext
choices.why: Denying them a pretext is worth more than two hours
choices.after: At 6 p.m., when Kennedy finished speaking, Havana was still quiet. The alarm went out that night, and the militia began assembling on the morning of the 23rd. That night radar tracked three American aircraft across Cuban airspace, but none of the batteries that could have fired were yet in position.

choices.text: Send only the regular army to its starting positions and hold off on the militia; no one knows how many days of a million pesos a day lie ahead
choices.why: In a long standoff the economy collapses first
choices.after: The 105,000 regulars were in position that night. The militia was not called out until the 24th, and in the meantime you thought more than once of the 300,000 of 1961. Alekseev said again and again that Cuba was slow to mobilize.

note.text: The mobilization figures (350,000, 72 hours, 105,000, a million pesos a day) survive as Raúl Castro’s words in Alekseev’s cable to Moscow of 23 October. That the combat alarm went out in the afternoon, before the speech, is Castro’s 1992 recollection; the time of about 4 p.m. comes from the historian Gilly. No original text of the order exists, so the substance of the cable has been set out in the form of an order. The times of the three airspace violations are those the Cuban representative gave the Security Council on the 23rd.

pressure.title: 350,000 Men and 72 Hours
pressure.text: On 17 April 1961, too, you threw in every man you had on the day you heard of the landing, and it was over within 72 hours. Ever since, you have believed the Americans would come back, so the notice of Kennedy’s “major statement” is not news to you but news you have been waiting for. There are 42,000 Soviet troops on the island, but their orders come from Moscow, and whatever Moscow has ordered has not yet reached Havana. Raúl’s figure is a million pesos a day, and in 1961 you counted 300,000 who could bear arms. Wait for the speech and you lose hours; don’t wait and you will be told Cuba moved first.

map.caption: Havana, Santiago in the east, and the American base at Guantánamo at the island’s eastern end.

FC-02.unknown: In Washington, Kennedy was preparing to speak at 7 p.m. Washington time. The United States had photographed the launch site at San Cristóbal on 14 October and spent six days in White House meetings weighing an air strike against a blockade. In Moscow the Presidium was holding off its decision until the text of the speech came in, and at 11:30 p.m. Moscow time on the 22nd Order No. 4/389 went out to the Soviet command: raise combat readiness, but leave out the missiles and the nuclear warheads. The next day Alekseev reported Cuba’s mobilization and rules of engagement to Moscow.

FC-03.title: International Gendarme
FC-03.clock: About 2 hours until the Security Council’s 1022nd meeting opens in New York (3 p.m. in Havana)

telegram.cls: Top Secret · Making Copies Prohibited · Copy No. 12
telegram.subject: Delivery of your Nos. 811 and 812–813
telegram.text: Your Nos. 811 and 812–813 delivered to F. Castro, Dorticós and Aragonés present. Also informed him of full text of Soviet government statement received via TASS, combat readiness measures for Soviet armed forces taken by defense minister, appointment of Marshal Grechko as representative of Warsaw Pact forces. / Castro thanked Soviet government for support, expressed confidence new American aggression plans will fail. Said U.S. at present lacks sufficient forces for surprise attack on Cuba. / Castro fully approves Soviet government’s tactics, tone of documents sent to him, and aim of exposing U.S. leaders before world opinion as international gendarme.

FC-03.event: Alekseev has brought documents from Moscow: a Soviet government statement and a letter from Khrushchev. The statement calls the American measures piracy and orders Soviet forces to combat readiness; the letter says that the choice of alliances is Cuba’s right. Nowhere is there any word of withdrawal. What the Soviet ships heading for the blockade line are to do, none of the documents says.
FC-03.scene: Alekseev read you the documents with Dorticós and Aragonés present. You answer without hesitation: the Soviet tactics are entirely right, the United States does not have the forces for a surprise attack at this moment, and exposing Kennedy as an international gendarme is the correct course. Then you add a few things. Since the Americans and the Cuban people both know Soviet troops are here anyway, Cuban units might be folded into the Soviet order of battle as divisions. The demand to strip the Guantánamo base of its legal basis could be put to work in propaganda. And there is the discipline of the Soviet “specialists.” Rowdiness in public places, panic and car accidents are setting Cubans talking. Raúl meant to hold a meeting on discipline with the Soviet commanders, but yesterday’s events put it off. You must decide what to ask of Moscow.

voices.text: Fidel, Moscow wants to hear that you are calm. I’ll pass on the idea about the units, but that the missiles stay under Soviet command has been a settled condition since May. Don’t make any more demands that touch that line.

Cuba isn’t in the Soviet statement. It reads as if this were a matter between the United States and the Soviet Union. Today García-Incháustegui speaks for Cuba in New York, but here in Havana the Cuban government must speak for itself too. Put Guantánamo in, and it becomes Cuba’s demand.

voices.who: Khrushchev (letter of 23 October, read out by Castro in 1992)
voices.text: The Republic of Cuba, like any other sovereign state, has every right to defend itself and to choose the alliances it wishes. The Soviet government has instructed the representatives of the Soviet armed forces in Cuba to take the appropriate measures and bring themselves to full combat readiness. The aggressive plans of the American imperialists will be thwarted.

choices.text: Issue a Cuban government statement first, separate from the Soviet one, rejecting the blockade and demanding withdrawal from Guantánamo in Cuba’s own name
choices.why: The moment this looks like a matter between two great powers, Cuba disappears
choices.after: The statement went out on the evening news. Alekseev said only that he would pass the Guantánamo passage on to Moscow as it stood, and he did not look pleased. That night you had to sit before the television cameras and say far more than the statement had.

choices.text: Answer that you fully support the Soviet line, and raise only the discipline of Soviet troops, formally, through Raúl
choices.why: Speaking with one voice leaves Washington no way to split the two
choices.after: Alekseev said he would pass your words on to Moscow as you had spoken them. The Soviet command agreed to hold a meeting of commanders with Raúl present. At 3 p.m. the Security Council met in New York, and García-Incháustegui read out the times of the three airspace violations. That night it was your turn to speak.

choices.text: Formally propose folding Cuban units into the Soviet order of battle, and in return demand a joint command that decides on antiaircraft fire together
choices.why: Cuba must have a say in every gun fired on the island
choices.after: Alekseev said only that he would pass it on. The Soviet command’s answer came that night, brought by General Pliyev himself.

note.text: This conversation survives in summary form in Alekseev’s cable of 23 October (Special Nos. 1643–1644); the cable’s header (classification, copy number, serial number) follows the English translation of the original. The Soviet government statement and Khrushchev’s letter of 23 October are confirmed only in the English translation Castro read out at the 1992 Havana conference, so they are given in gist. The condition that the missiles stay under Soviet command is in the original of the Presidium notes of 21 May.

FC-03.unknown: In Moscow, at 10 a.m. (2 a.m. in Havana), the Presidium had already ordered the ships still outside the blockade line to turn back. That decision appeared neither in the Soviet government statement nor in Khrushchev’s letter. Alekseev reported this conversation to Moscow in cable Special Nos. 1643–1644.

FC-04.title: Good Rockets and Bad Rockets
FC-04.clock: About 12 hours until the quarantine line takes effect, per American radio (9 a.m. on the 24th)
FC-04.event: At 4 p.m. in New York, at the Security Council’s 1022nd meeting, the Cuban representative, García-Incháustegui, said there were two kinds of military bases and two kinds of rockets in the world: good bases and bad bases, good rockets and bad rockets, and the United States government decided which were good and which were bad. In the evening American radio reported that Kennedy had signed the quarantine proclamation and that it would take effect in the morning. Moscow is silent.
FC-04.scene: Before you sit down in front of the cameras, there is one thing to decide: how to speak of the missiles. The Soviet statement said the weapons were purely defensive, and the TASS statement in September said the Soviet Union had no need for bases beyond its borders. Last night Kennedy held up photographs and called them medium-range missiles. Deny it, and you stay in step with the Soviets but lie in the face of the photographs; confirm it, and you overturn the Soviet statement. The foreign ambassadors in Havana will take down your every word tonight and send it home. The speech may run for hours, and you will speak without a text.

voices.who: Mario García-Incháustegui (UN representative, 1022nd meeting of the Security Council)
voices.text: The Cuban people are a people ready to die for their independence and sovereignty, and those who are ready to die have the inalienable right to make their voice heard by those who are leading mankind to catastrophe.

At the UN Cuba has held to one line: neither deny nor confirm what kind of weapons they are, and say that a sovereign state has the right to whatever weapons it wishes. Step off that line tonight, and our delegation in New York will have nothing to say tomorrow.

Say again what I said at the General Assembly on 8 October: if the United States guarantees, in word and deed, that it will not attack, Cuba will need neither weapons nor an army. That is the only condition Cuba has put forward, and there are delegates at the UN who remember it.

choices.text: Keep step with the Soviet statement: say there are no offensive weapons in Cuba and dismiss the photographs as an American fabrication
choices.why: The moment you say something different from your patron, the alliance wobbles
choices.after: The words went out, but the photographs remained. Later, when Stevenson held up the photographs in the Security Council, the Cuban representative had no answer. In 1992 you would say Cuba never took part in that “game”; on this path you cannot say so.

choices.text: Neither deny nor confirm what weapons they are, and speak of sovereignty; refuse UN observers and call the blockade piracy
choices.why: Cuba’s strength lies in standing where it neither lies nor gives the secret away
choices.after: The speech went on late into the night. The weapons are defensive; Cuba decides what weapons it will have; no UN observers will be let in; the blockade is piracy. You did not deny the word “missiles.” At 9 the next morning the quarantine line took effect.

choices.text: Confirm outright that Soviet strategic rockets are in Cuba, and make it public that they result from an agreement between a sovereign state and its ally
choices.why: In a fight the side that hides loses, the side that speaks first wins
choices.after: Alekseev was waiting outside the studio. Moscow was still using the word “defensive.”

note.text: The full text of the 23 October speech could not be obtained for this research (access to the Cuban speech archive was blocked). Its content has been reconstructed from Dutch Ambassador Boissevain’s report of 25 October, Alekseev’s cable and Castro’s 1992 recollection; the time of the speech has not been confirmed. García-Incháustegui’s remarks in the Security Council are from the original UN record.
note.src: WC/UMD 91504; WC/UMD 111915; Castro 1992 [secondary]; S/PV.1022 §104; Phase 1 issue 18

FC-04.unknown: Moscow said nothing in public, but that morning the Presidium had already ordered the ships outside the blockade line to turn back. In Washington Kennedy signed the quarantine proclamation, to take effect at 10 a.m. Washington time on the 24th. On the 25th the Dutch ambassador in Havana, Boissevain, reported home that Khrushchev had denied it but Castro had not.

FC-05.place: Havana, high command of the Revolutionary Armed Forces
FC-05.title: Under the Blockade
FC-05.clock: Quarantine line takes effect; no telling when the next low-level flight will come

telegram.from: García-Incháustegui, Cuba’s representative to the UN (statement at the 1022nd meeting of the Security Council)
telegram.to: The President and members of the Security Council
telegram.subject: The American naval blockade and Cuban sovereignty
telegram.text: Two kinds of military bases in the world, it seems, and two kinds of rockets. Good bases and bad bases, good rockets and bad rockets, and which are good and which are bad is for the United States government to decide. / Two weeks ago the President of Cuba declared from the rostrum of the General Assembly: if the United States can give proof by word and deed that it will commit no aggression against Cuba, Cuba solemnly declares it will need neither weapons nor an army.

FC-05.event: At 9 a.m. the quarantine line (the naval cordon that stopped ships bound for Cuba) took effect. Where the Soviet ships heading for the blockade line are now, and what they are doing, neither Moscow nor Alekseev has said. At 11:30 a.m. the day before, two American fighters passed over a Soviet missile regiment at 100–150 meters, and the Cuban lookouts could only watch. Soviet surface-to-air missiles are weapons for targets above 1,000 meters.
FC-05.scene: The Soviet positions lie open to the sky: missile launch sites, surface-to-air missile sites, airfields. When American aircraft fly at 100 meters, Soviet air defense can do nothing, and what the Cuban artillery has is conventional antiaircraft guns. Raúl has spread out a map. Fifty antiaircraft batteries are held in reserve, and that is the whole of the Cuban forces’ reserve. Spread them around the Soviet positions and the air defense of Havana and Santiago grows thin; leave them where they are, and one morning the Soviet missiles and the 40,000 men guarding them could vanish in a single surprise attack. Then everything Cuba has taken on would have been for nothing. The Security Council sits again today in New York, and the words of 8 October that your delegation read out yesterday are still in that chamber.

voices.who: Raúl Castro (minister of the Revolutionary Armed Forces)
voices.text: It’s all 50 batteries. Send half and they can’t protect any site; send them all and we leave the sky over Havana to the Soviet missiles. But their missiles are for planes that fly high. What comes in low is the Cuban gunner’s job.

voices.who: Che Guevara (by telephone from Pinar del Río)
voices.text: Over the launch site at San Cristóbal the planes go by as if they were skimming the roofs. The Soviet soldiers raise their heads out of the trenches and watch. Send us the batteries. If they only watch, the Cuban soldiers will only watch too.

Yesterday in New York García-Incháustegui read out again what I said on 8 October: given a guarantee of no aggression, we need neither weapons nor an army. Wherever you put the batteries, those words must not sound empty. But construction at the launch sites is the Soviets’ business; Cuba can’t promise anything on their behalf.

choices.text: Keep the batteries for the air defense of Havana and the major cities, and leave the Soviets to guard their positions with their own means
choices.why: The Cuban forces’ first duty is the sky over Cuban heads
choices.after: American planes came over the Soviet positions every day, and Soviet soldiers looked up at them from beside missiles they could not fire. Alekseev twice raised the lack of Cuban cooperation, and word came from Pliyev’s side that he had asked Moscow for authority to fire on low-flying aircraft.

choices.text: Leave the Soviets to protect themselves, and put the Cuban forces into strengthening the coastal and road defenses against a landing
choices.why: The missiles are the Soviets’ affair; stopping a landing is Cuba’s
choices.after: Trenches were dug along the coast, as in 1961. But the missile sites were left without conventional antiaircraft guns, and on the 26th it was Pliyev’s side that asked whether Cuban batteries could be sent.

choices.text: Deploy all 50 reserve antiaircraft batteries around the Soviet missile and air defense sites to stop the low-level flights
choices.why: If the missiles vanish in a surprise attack, everything has been for nothing
choices.after: The batteries began moving that night. Later you would write to Khrushchev that on 24 October the Cuban forces mobilized 50 antiaircraft batteries, their entire reserve at the time, to cover the Soviet positions. There was no order to fire yet. The gunners could only watch the planes go over.

note.text: The deployment of 50 antiaircraft batteries is in the original of Castro’s letter to Khrushchev of 28 October. The Soviet missile division’s halted move and the low-level pass of 23 October are in division commander Statsenko’s report of December 1962; the turning back of the Soviet ships is in the Presidium notes of 23 October. That Soviet surface-to-air missiles were weapons for targets above 1,000 meters is Castro’s 1992 recollection. U Thant’s appeal is taken from the original UN record.

FC-05.unknown: The Soviet ships heading for the blockade line had already turned back the day before, on the Presidium’s orders, and Washington confirmed it only that morning. The Soviet missile division had been choosing new positions for its launch sites but had halted for lack of spare parts. That evening, at the Security Council’s 1024th meeting in New York, U Thant made an urgent appeal to the President and Prime Minister of Cuba to suspend the construction and development of major military facilities in Cuba during the negotiations.

FC-06.title: 100 Meters
FC-06.clock: About 18 hours until the next morning’s American low-level flights

telegram.from: Commander-in-Chief of the Revolutionary Armed Forces
telegram.to: Command of Soviet forces in Cuba
telegram.subject: Antiaircraft fire on low-flying aircraft
telegram.text: Low-level flights by U.S. aircraft over Cuban airspace no longer tolerable. / From 27 October Cuban antiaircraft batteries will open fire on aircraft intruding at low altitude. / Soviet command so notified as it should be aware.

FC-06.event: American radio reported that on the morning of the 26th the U.S. Navy stopped and searched the Lebanese-flagged freighter Marucla at the quarantine line. From Moscow nothing has come for you since the letter of the 23rd. What you know is that American planes come every morning at 100 meters, photograph the Soviet positions and go home, and that from today Soviet air defense has permission to switch on its radars.
FC-06.scene: At the Soviet headquarters at El Chico you met the Soviet officers. They said they were ready. You told them what the low-level flights meant. The planes that take photographs and the planes that drop bombs come in at the same height along the same route. If one morning they come with bombs instead of cameras, positions waiting with their radars off and their batteries without orders to fire will be wiped out at a stroke. Under the agreement there are two armies and two commands on the island, and the Cuban forces are commanded by Cuba. For three days the gunners have done nothing but watch planes pass overhead, and Raúl cannot promise how long their morale will hold. If you order them to fire, Cuba fires the first shot; if you don’t, the planes come again tomorrow morning.

voices.who: Raúl Castro (minister of the Revolutionary Armed Forces)
voices.text: For three days the gunners have only looked up at the planes. Tell them not to fire tomorrow morning too, and after that their hands will be slow even when the order comes. An order to fire is, before it is anything else, what keeps a battery a battery.

Fidel, U Thant sent his second appeal from New York yesterday, and Kennedy and Khrushchev have both answered. Just when talks are about to begin, if a Cuban shell hits an American plane, the talks are finished. Can’t you wait one more day?

From today our air defense switches on its radars. Our surface-to-air missiles cannot catch targets below 1,000 meters. If the Cuban batteries will take the low level, the command will not object. But Soviet forces fire on Moscow’s orders.
If we wanted to avoid the danger of a surprise attack, the Cuban artillerymen had to be given the order to fire.

choices.text: Notify the Soviet command that from the morning of the 27th Cuban batteries will open fire on American aircraft coming in low
choices.why: Firing the first shot is less dangerous than waiting for a surprise attack
choices.after: The notification went out then and there. Pliyev said he would report the Cuban decision to Moscow, and raised no objection. That night you went to the Soviet embassy to write a letter.

choices.text: Keep the rule against firing first, and hold back a few days more while U Thant’s talks get moving
choices.why: Cuba must not be the country that fires the first shell on the day talks begin
choices.after: The batteries were silent again the next morning. Raúl reported that artillery commanders were asking to have their orders confirmed. Soviet air defense switched on its radars, and what that would mean the next day even they did not know.

choices.text: Ask Soviet air defense to intercept the low-flying planes and keep the Cuban batteries on standby; if Soviet weapons fire, the decision is Soviet
choices.why: Responsibility belongs with the owner of the missiles
choices.after: Pliyev said he would ask Moscow. Since the surface-to-air missiles could not catch low-flying aircraft, the request in effect came down to the high-altitude reconnaissance planes, and no answer came from Moscow. That night you went to the Soviet embassy.

note.text: The decision of 26 October to open fire is confirmed only by Castro’s 1992 recollection and by Soviet reports (in scholarly works quoting Pliyev’s cable); the only Cuban military orders confirmed in the original are those of 17 and 18 November. The wording of the notification sets out the content of the recollection in the form of a notice. That Soviet air defense was permitted to switch on its radars from 26 October is in the original of division commander Statsenko’s report.

map.caption: The headquarters of the Soviet Group of Forces was at El Chico, on the southwestern outskirts of Havana.

FC-06.unknown: In Moscow that evening Khrushchev sent Kennedy a long letter proposing that they untie “the knot” together. The night before, a Soviet submarine had surfaced in the Atlantic with engine trouble and been spotted by an American carrier group. Pliyev reported to Moscow that the Cubans expected a night air strike and had decided to open antiaircraft fire if attacked.

FC-07.place: Havana, residence of Soviet Ambassador Alekseev
FC-07.title: A Letter Rewritten Dozens of Times
FC-07.clock: About 3 hours until the American morning reconnaissance

telegram.cls: Top Secret · Making Copies Prohibited · Copy No. 12
telegram.subject: Letter from F. Castro
telegram.text: F. Castro at embassy composing personal letter to N. S. Khrushchev; will transmit immediately on completion. / In F. Castro’s judgment intervention almost inevitable, within approximately 24–72 hours.

FC-07.event: What has reached you are reports that American landing forces are massing in Florida, and more reconnaissance planes every day. Moscow has said nothing since the letter of the 23rd, and apart from news that U Thant is trying to broker something in New York, you cannot tell what is passing between the two great powers. You have decided to go without sleep tonight.
FC-07.scene: At 2 a.m. Dorticós telephoned Alekseev to say the Prime Minister was on his way. You stayed at the house until 7 in the morning, dictating, correcting and dictating again, dozens of times over. The first part of the letter is clear: an attack is almost certain within 24 to 72 hours; there are two possibilities, the likelier an air strike on specific targets, the less likely but possible a full invasion; the morale of the Cuban people is high, and they will fight any attack. The second part is your own opinion. It concerns what the Soviet Union should do if the second case comes, if the imperialists invade to occupy Cuba. For a long while Alekseev could not grasp what that sentence meant and asked you, and you answered that you did not mean to say it outright, but that in the event of aggression against Cuba they must not wait for the enemy’s treachery and first strike but get ahead of it. You put the chance that no attack would come at 5 in 100. The letter is not yet sealed.

voices.who: Aleksandr Alekseev (the night’s conversation, as recorded in his cable of 2 November)
voices.text: For a long time I couldn’t make out what that complicated sentence of yours meant. So I asked you straight out: are you saying the Soviet Union should strike the enemy first with nuclear weapons? You said no, you didn’t mean to say that outright. Only in the event of aggression against Cuba.

Comrade Prime Minister, think how Moscow will read that sentence. What it means written in Havana and what it means read in Moscow may not be the same. Write in the condition, in the event of an invasion, again and again.

voices.who: Fidel Castro (opening of the letter dated 26 October)
voices.text: Given the analysis of the situation and the reports in our possession, I consider that the aggression is almost imminent within the next 24 or 72 hours. There are two possible variants: the first and likeliest one is an air attack against certain targets with the limited objective of destroying them; the second, less probable although possible, is invasion.

choices.text: Hold back the letter and send Moscow only the warning of imminent attack, through Alekseev’s cable; leave your opinion as spoken words
choices.why: Words put in writing cannot be taken back
choices.after: Only cable No. 1666 went out. Your opinion survived only in Alekseev’s memory, and Khrushchev never read it. At 7 a.m. you left the embassy for the high command. Three hours later something fell from the sky over Banes in the east.

choices.text: Send the revised letter as it stands, with both your judgment that attack is imminent and your opinion on what the Soviet Union must do in the event of an invasion
choices.why: An ally that hides what its patron needs to know is no ally
choices.after: The letter went to Moscow in the morning, in Alekseev’s cipher. Four days later, from Khrushchev’s reply, you would learn that he had read the sentence as a proposal that the Soviet Union strike first with nuclear weapons, and you would tell Alekseev you had meant not a preemptive strike during the crisis but what to do if Cuba were invaded. Thirty years later in Havana you would say it had been meant as a warning.

choices.text: Write into the letter a request that, in the event of invasion, the local commander be given authority to use the Soviet tactical nuclear weapons on the island
choices.why: The weapons that can finish a landing force on the beaches are already on the island
choices.after: Taking down the request, Alekseev stopped writing for the first time. The very fact that the Cuban prime minister knew those weapons were on the island, he said, was something he would have to report.

note.text: The letter is dated 26 October and was written between 2 and 7 a.m. on the 27th (Alekseev’s cable of 2 November). The Soviet side calls it “the cable of 27 October.” The original of the passage on what the Soviet Union should do in the event of an invasion (an English translation of the Spanish) is public, but here it is given only in gist, with its document number. There are two readings. Khrushchev, in his replies of 28 and 30 October, read it as a proposal for a preemptive nuclear strike (in a note beforehand he wrote “out of despair”); Castro told Alekseev on 31 October that he had meant not a preemptive strike during the crisis but the case of an invasion of Cuba, with Soviet people dying alongside Cubans, and at the 1992 conference he explained that it had been meant as a warning. Both readings are given here.
note.src: NSA 621026; PBS jfk-attack; WC/UMD 115063; WC/UMD 115064; WC/UMD 112640; WC/UMD 300937; Phase 1 issue 4

pressure.title: Dictation Before Dawn
pressure.text: The letter is being written not at the high command but at Alekseev’s house, between 2 and 7 in the morning. Before that, in cipher cable Special No. 1666, Alekseev had already told Moscow of your judgment that an attack was imminent, and you put the chance of no attack at 5 in 100. The first part of the letter gives an attack within 24 to 72 hours and its two possibilities; the second gives your opinion that in the event of an invasion the Soviet Union must not wait for the enemy’s first strike. When Alekseev asked whether that sentence meant a preemptive nuclear strike, you answered that you did not mean to say so outright. Turned into cipher, the letter will take hours to reach Moscow, and who will read that sentence there, and how, you cannot know. What you have assumed ever since Playa Girón is a long war costing hundreds of thousands of lives.
pressure.src: WC/UMD 115063; WC/UMD 115064; NSA 621026; WC/UMD 300937; WC/UMD 112640; Phase 1 issue 4

FC-07.unknown: In Washington, on the evening of the 26th, the White House was reading Khrushchev’s letter of that day, and the ABC newsman John Scali heard from Fomin of the Soviet embassy a proposal to trade a pledge not to invade for withdrawal of the missiles. In Moscow that morning the Presidium was preparing a second letter adding a demand for the American missiles in Turkey. Khrushchev read your letter as a proposal for a preemptive nuclear strike, and on 30 October he noted that Castro had sent it “out of despair.”

FC-08.place: Havana, high command of the Revolutionary Armed Forces
FC-08.title: Aircraft of Unknown Nationality
FC-08.clock: Moments after the shootdown report; day one of the 24–72 hours in your letter
FC-08.event: In the morning the American low-level reconnaissance planes came in as on any other day, and this time Cuban batteries fired on them. At about 10:20 a.m. word came that over Banes in the east a U.S. Air Force U-2 flying at 20,000 meters had been hit by a Soviet surface-to-air missile and brought down. The Cuban forces had no part in it, and no Cuban battery has a weapon that reaches that height. Who gave the order to fire, the Soviets are not saying. Since about 9 a.m. Radio Moscow has been reading a new letter from Khrushchev, and in it is a proposal to trade the American missiles in Turkey for the Soviet missiles in Cuba.
FC-08.scene: The reports came in two streams. One said Cuban batteries had fired on low-flying planes in the morning and the planes had turned back; the other, that Soviet air defense had shot down a high-altitude reconnaissance plane. The Soviets are asking how the Cuban government will announce it, and Alekseev, saying it is Moscow’s wish, has asked for restraint. You answered that you understood the gravity of the act. But you also answered that, with the troops’ fighting spirit running high, and the United States having tried yesterday to make official its privilege of violating Cuban airspace at any hour of the day or night, the step could not have been avoided. On the radio there is talk of Turkey, something no one ever discussed with Cuba. The wreckage of the downed plane lies scattered at Banes, and Raúl has sent photographs from the east.

voices.who: Aleksandr Alekseev (Castro’s words as reported in his cable of 27 October)
voices.text: Castro said he understood the gravity of this step, but that, given the fighting spirit of the troops and the American warnings, the Cuban comrades could not but take such a step.

It was the Soviet missile unit at Banes that fired. Our batteries fired at the low-flying planes this morning and hit nothing. How will you announce it? Say the Soviets did it and Moscow is in trouble; say the Cubans did it and it’s a lie.

voices.who: Che Guevara (by telephone from Pinar del Río)
voices.text: The gunners in the west fired for the first time this morning. The planes turned back and no one was hit, but the batteries are batteries now. If you order a ceasefire, what am I to tell them?

choices.text: Order the Cuban batteries to cease fire and urge restraint on the Soviet command too; on the day a Turkey deal is on the table there is no reason to fire again
choices.why: A shootdown on the day talks open will come back on Cuba
choices.after: The batteries fell silent at noon. All afternoon there was no telling whether a retaliatory strike would come. In the evening Alekseev came again.

choices.text: Keep firing, but wait for Moscow’s answer before announcing the shootdown; it is not for Cuba to say first who fired
choices.why: Let the Soviet Union speak first about what its own weapons did
choices.after: No answer came from Moscow, and the American papers had it first: a U.S. Air Force plane missing over Cuba. Only in the evening did the Cuban government announce that it had shot down an aircraft of unknown nationality.

choices.text: Keep firing, announce in the Cuban government’s name that an aircraft of unknown nationality has been shot down, and tell Alekseev it was unavoidable
choices.why: Whoever’s weapon fired, the decision to defend the airspace is Cuba’s
choices.after: The announcement went out during the day. American radio reported that a U.S. Air Force plane had failed to return from a flight over Cuba, but of how Washington would answer, nothing could be heard. In the afternoon it was time to answer U Thant’s letter.

note.text: The chain of command behind the U-2 shootdown is disputed. General Garbuz testified that with Pliyev absent, Grechko and he made the decision; Malinovsky’s report of 28 October names no one. The Cuban forces had no part in the shootdown. The Cuban batteries’ fire on low-flying aircraft appears in Castro’s 1992 recollection and in his letter of 28 October. The time of the shootdown converts the 6:20 p.m. Moscow time in Malinovsky’s report to Havana time.
note.src: WC/UMD 110999; WC/UMD 107028; Garbuz 1992 [secondary]; Castro 1992 [secondary]; Phase 1 issue 2

pressure.title: Who Fired First
pressure.text: The order to fire was given a day earlier, and its roots lie in the 50 batteries of 24 October. It was you who spread the Cuban forces’ entire reserve around the Soviet positions, and you who decided not to wait for a surprise attack with the radars off. Raúl could not vouch for the morale of gunners who had spent three days watching planes pass overhead, and you told Alekseev the troops’ fighting spirit was running high. It was Soviet air defense that brought down the high-altitude reconnaissance plane, and the Cuban forces had no part in that decision; but the Soviets will not say who gave the order, and there is no knowing whose shootdown Washington will take it to be. The talk of Turkey on the radio is something never discussed with Cuba, and the official text of that letter has not yet reached even the embassy.
pressure.src: WC/UMD 110999; NSA 19621028caslet; WC/UMD 114504; Phase 1 issue 2; Phase 1 issue 19

map.caption: On the morning of 27 October an American U-2 was shot down near Banes in eastern Cuba.

FC-08.unknown: The decision to shoot down the U-2 was taken, in Pliyev’s absence, by Generals Grechko and Garbuz of Soviet air defense, without authorization from Moscow. The pilot, Major Anderson, was killed. At the same hour an American U-2 from Alaska strayed into Soviet airspace. At 4 p.m. in Washington the ExComm received the report of the shootdown, and McNamara spoke of an air strike on Monday followed by an invasion, but that night Kennedy held off retaliation.

FC-09.title: All but Becoming a Victim
FC-09.clock: U Thant’s letter still unanswered; a few hours since the shootdown over Banes

telegram.from: U Thant, acting secretary-general of the United Nations
telegram.to: His Excellency Fidel Castro, Prime Minister of the Revolutionary Government of Cuba
telegram.cc: García-Incháustegui, permanent representative of Cuba to the UN
telegram.subject: Appeal to suspend construction of major military facilities
telegram.text: I trust that Ambassador García-Incháustegui has conveyed to Your Excellency the appeal I made to you and President Dorticós in the Security Council on 24 October. I then recalled the words of the President from the rostrum of the General Assembly on 8 October. / I have received fairly encouraging responses from the President of the United States and the Chairman of the Council of Ministers of the USSR to my appeal for negotiations and a peaceful settlement. / Your Excellency could make a significant contribution to the peace of the world at this present critical juncture by directing that the construction and development of major military facilities and installations in Cuba, and especially installations designed to launch medium-range and intermediate-range ballistic missiles, be suspended during the period of negotiations which are now under way. / I should greatly appreciate an affirmative reply to this appeal very urgently.

FC-09.event: What has reached you in Havana is the letter U Thant sent yesterday. It asks you to halt construction. The construction is Soviet. Since the plane came down over Banes this morning there has been no sign of how the Americans will answer, and Alekseev has yet to bring any explanation of the Turkey proposal Radio Moscow read out.
FC-09.scene: Foreign Minister Roa has brought a draft reply. U Thant has quoted once more what Dorticós told the UN General Assembly on 8 October: if the United States guaranteed in word and deed that it would not attack, Cuba would need neither weapons nor an army. Cuba said it, and Cuba cannot take it back. But the blockade remains, and the United States claims the right to decide what weapons Cuba may have and what relations it may keep with the Soviet Union. You want three things in one document: that Cuba is ready to discuss all its differences with the United States, in cooperation with the UN; that it flatly rejects the blockade and the American claim to decide; and that U Thant should come to Havana if he wishes.

voices.text: Comrade Prime Minister, if we simply refuse, we forget that some 50 non-aligned delegations stand behind U Thant. Accept with conditions: Cuba can accept a compromise if threats and acts of aggression, the blockade included, stop while the talks go on. And invite him to Havana. While the secretary-general is in Havana, no bombs will fall.

What I said on 8 October carried one condition: a guarantee not to attack. Don’t withdraw that condition. That U Thant is holding on to those words means the condition Cuba laid down has become the UN’s condition.

voices.who: Fidel Castro (reply to U Thant, 27 October)
voices.text: Cuba can do anything that is asked of it, except agree to become a victim or renounce the rights that belong to every sovereign state.

choices.text: Reply that Cuba is ready to accept a compromise on condition that threats and aggressive acts, the blockade included, stop, and invite U Thant to Havana
choices.why: Setting Cuba’s own conditions between refusal and acceptance is what sovereignty means
choices.after: The reply went to New York through García-Incháustegui, and the UN released it that day with U Thant’s letter as press release SG/1359. The next day U Thant wrote that he gladly accepted the invitation, and he set his departure for the 30th. In the evening Alekseev came with Khrushchev’s second letter.

choices.text: Accept without conditions: agree to halt construction during the talks, and signal willingness to accept UN observers
choices.why: Taking U Thant’s hand is the only way to hold off Washington’s bombs
choices.after: The reply was welcomed in New York, and a question came back from Moscow: the construction was Soviet, so how could Cuba promise to halt it? You answered that Cuba could speak for what happened on Cuban soil. In the evening Alekseev came with Khrushchev’s second letter.

choices.text: Refuse outright: to discuss halting construction under blockade is to discuss surrender, and the UN must deal with the blockade first
choices.why: Talks that begin by accepting the blockade are not talks
choices.after: The reply was short, and the non-aligned delegations in New York were disappointed. U Thant sent word through the delegation that he would go to Havana all the same. In the evening Alekseev came with Khrushchev’s second letter.

note.text: The full texts of U Thant’s letter of 26 October and Castro’s reply of 27 October are in UN press release SG/1359 (the UN’s English translation of the Spanish original). The two reports of the Brazilian ambassador, Bastian Pinto (5:45 and 7:15 p.m.), are English translations of the originals in Wilson Center documents. The number of non-aligned delegations survives in the Security Council records as “some 50 member states,” in statements by Riad and Quaison-Sackey (S/PV.1024 §62, S/PV.1025 §91).

FC-09.unknown: That afternoon in Washington the ExComm spent hours deciding which of Khrushchev’s two letters to answer, and Robert Kennedy was to meet the Soviet ambassador, Dobrynin, in the evening. In the Atlantic American destroyers were forcing a Soviet submarine to the surface with practice depth charges. That evening the Brazilian ambassador in Havana, Bastian Pinto, wrote home that the absence of any talk of inspection in Cuba’s reply might be a sign of softening.

FC-10.title: Radio Moscow
FC-10.clock: Minutes into the broadcast; no letter for you yet

telegram.from: Radio Moscow (reading of Khrushchev’s letter to Kennedy)
telegram.to: J. F. Kennedy, President of the United States
telegram.subject: Reply to the letter of 27 October
telegram.text: In addition to the earlier instructions on the discontinuation of further work on the weapons construction sites, the Soviet Government has given a new order to dismantle the arms which you described as offensive, and to crate and return them to the Soviet Union. / We are ready to reach agreement to enable United Nations representatives to verify the dismantling of these means. / I regard with respect and trust the statement you made that there would be no invasion of Cuba.

FC-10.event: Last night Alekseev brought Khrushchev’s second letter. It proposed trading the American missiles in Turkey for the Soviet missiles in Cuba, and Moscow asked you to declare publicly that work on the special weapons inside Cuba was banned. You said the letter had been written with great diplomatic skill, but also that some officers and some of the population were confused; you answered that today you would publish the full text and explain it yourself, but that any ban on construction had to be tied to Guantánamo. Before you could give that explanation, the radio spoke first.
FC-10.scene: Radio Moscow is reading Khrushchev’s letter. It is addressed to Kennedy. The weapons will be dismantled and sent back to the Soviet Union; the UN will verify it; the United States will not invade. Cuba appears only as the object of the terms. No one consulted you. The letter Alekseev brought last night offered a trade for Turkey, and nowhere was there any word of withdrawal without conditions; in Khrushchev’s letter of the 23rd you read only the will to fight. Raúl comes in, then Dorticós, then Roa, who has just hung up on New York. There is still no letter addressed to you. No one in the room shows any sign of relief. What shows is anger, and the sense that Cuba has become a piece on someone else’s board. In the streets the militia are still in their trenches, and the gunners at the Soviet positions fired for the first time yesterday. You must decide what to say today, and to whom.

voices.who: Raúl Roa (foreign minister, to the Yugoslav and Brazilian ambassadors the same day)
voices.text: When lives are at stake, one has to say something. This declaration is addressed not only to the United States but to the Soviet Union as well. It is meant to show both of them that Cuba is not a toy in the hands of the great powers and must have a voice in the coming negotiations. These demands will be subject to negotiation; I repeat, subject to negotiation.

voices.who: Raúl Castro (minister of the Revolutionary Armed Forces)
voices.text: What do we tell the soldiers? Yesterday they fired for the first time, and today we hear the missiles are leaving. Someone has to tell them what they were defending. The Cuban government’s word has to go out before the Soviet government’s.

If we condemn the Soviet decision in public, no one will be happier than the Americans. But if we say we support it, Cuba becomes the country that approved a decision it was never consulted on. Putting forward Cuba’s demands in Cuba’s own name is the way between the two.

Commander in Chief, I have nothing to say today. Whatever we tell the Cuban people, it must be Cuba that decides it. The fewer the conditions, the stronger they are. If there are five, all five must be Cuba’s own.

choices.text: Issue a short statement supporting the Soviet decision, and give your explanation on television once Khrushchev’s letter has arrived
choices.why: Allies do not open their rifts in front of the enemy
choices.after: The statement went out at noon. The streets took it quietly, and Alekseev called that quiet “confusion.” Khrushchev’s letter came in the afternoon, and it urged patience and firmness over yesterday’s shootdown.

choices.text: Say nothing today. Hold back any explanation until you have read Khrushchev’s letter and Mikoyan, or someone, comes to explain
choices.why: Words spoken in ignorance are of no use to either side
choices.after: Havana heard the news from Radio Moscow and the Miami stations, and the Cuban government kept silent. Staff of the Chinese embassy gave blood in the streets and talked of resisting on Cuba’s own strength. Khrushchev’s letter, which came in the afternoon, urged patience and firmness.

choices.text: Proclaim five points in the name of the Cuban government: an end to the economic blockade, to subversion, to pirate attacks and to violations of Cuban airspace, and withdrawal from Guantánamo
choices.why: A country left out of the decision must state its terms first if it is not to be left out of the negotiations
choices.after: The declaration went out that day, and the next morning it ran on the front page of Revolución beside the report of Khrushchev’s withdrawal order. Roa told the Yugoslav and Brazilian ambassadors that it was aimed at Khrushchev more than at Kennedy. Khrushchev’s letter, which came in the afternoon, urged patience and firmness over yesterday’s shootdown.

note.text: Khrushchev’s letter to Kennedy was broadcast in English at 5 p.m. Moscow time (10 a.m. in Havana; American daylight saving time ended that day, putting Havana and New York on the same clock). That does not fit the “around noon” of the 1992 recollections, and the stage 1 report left the point open. The broadcast text gives the relevant passages of the original letter (FRUS VI d68). This research did not find the Spanish original of the five points; they were checked against the English translation Castro read out in 1992 and the summaries by the Dutch ambassador and by Gilly (excerpt grade). The conversation with Alekseev on the evening of 27 October is in the English translation of his original cable.
note.src: FRUS VI d68; WC/UMD 110999; WC/UMD 115549; Castro 1992 [secondary]; Gilly [secondary]; Stage 1 issue 12

pressure.title: A Deal Heard on the Radio
pressure.text: You learned of Khrushchev’s decision not from a letter but from Radio Moscow, and no letter addressed to you has yet come. When you accepted the missiles in May, you put strengthening the socialist camp first and the defense of Cuba second, and said you would take even a thousand if need be. Weapons accepted on those terms have been bargained away without consulting Cuba, and no one in the leadership shows any sign of relief. Roa says Cuba must show the Soviet Union, not just the United States, that it is no plaything of the great powers. In the streets the militia are still in their trenches, and you have not yet ordered the gunners who fired for the first time yesterday to cease fire. Whether the American low-level planes will come again today, and whether the landing forces in Florida are still there after the broadcast of a settlement, you cannot yet tell.
pressure.src: Castro 1992 [secondary]; WC/UMD 115468; WC/UMD 115348; NSA 19621028khrlet; Stage 1 issue 12

FC-10.unknown: In Moscow Khrushchev had decided on the withdrawal without consulting Cuba and put his reply to Kennedy on the radio; the letter to you went to the embassy afterward. The night before, in Washington, Robert Kennedy had told Dobrynin that the American missiles in Turkey would be removed within a few months, though not as part of any public bargain. Some historians believe your letter, which reached Moscow on the morning of the 27th, gave Khrushchev the sense that events were slipping out of control and hastened his decision to withdraw.

FC-11.title: Patience, Firmness, and Even More Firmness
FC-11.clock: No American low-level flights today; no telling about tomorrow morning. About 40 hours until U Thant arrives (the 30th)

telegram.subject: On the letter of 27 October to Kennedy and yesterday’s shootdown
telegram.text: Our message of 27 October to President Kennedy allows the question to be settled in your favor, to defend Cuba from invasion and prevent war. Kennedy’s reply offers assurances that the United States will not invade Cuba with its own forces, nor permit its allies to carry out an invasion. / At this turning point in the crisis, I advise you not to be carried away by sentiment, and to show firmness. I understand your indignation at the aggressive actions of the United States and its violations of the elementary norms of international law. / Now that an agreement is within sight, the Pentagon is searching for a pretext to frustrate it. That is why it is organizing the provocative flights. Yesterday you shot down one of them, although earlier you did not shoot them down when they overflew your territory. The aggressors will take advantage of such a step for their own purposes. / Therefore I would like to advise you in a friendly manner to show patience, firmness and even more firmness. Naturally, if there is an invasion it will be necessary to repulse it by every means. But we must not allow ourselves to be carried away by provocations. / We will do everything possible to stabilize the situation in Cuba, defend Cuba against invasion and assure you the possibility of peacefully building socialism.

FC-11.event: Word has come from the delegation in New York that U Thant has accepted your invitation and will arrive in Havana on the 30th. Since morning not one American low-level plane has come in, but what that means you cannot tell. Despite the broadcast of a settlement, there is no report of American forces pulling back from Florida.
FC-11.scene: Khrushchev’s letter has come by way of Alekseev. Yesterday you shot one down; before that you did not fire. You know it was not Cuba that brought the plane down, and Khrushchev must know it too. But it was you who gave the order to fire, and without that order the gunners would have been sitting with their radars off, waiting for a surprise attack. You want to explain all this in your reply: the 50 batteries of 24 October, why the order to fire had to be given, and how yesterday the United States tried to make official its privilege of violating Cuban airspace at any hour of the day or night. Then comes the decision. Will you order the batteries to cease fire? If so, for how long? And will you accept, on Cuban soil, the verification Moscow has promised the UN? What exactly Moscow has promised the UN, you know only from one line in the broadcast.

voices.text: Fidel, Moscow wants two things. That the batteries don’t fire, and that U Thant gets to see the launchers. The second concerns Soviet weapons, so Moscow seems to think the Soviet side can answer for it. If you say no first, things get complicated.

voices.who: Raúl Castro (minister of the Revolutionary Armed Forces)
voices.text: The cease-fire must hold only while the negotiations go on. A cease-fire with no time limit means taking back the air defense we declared yesterday. And if those planes come in at 100 meters again, the gunners will fire without stopping to ask about orders. An order can hold them back for only so long.

Inspection is a question not of missiles but of sovereignty. The Soviets offering to show their own weapons is one thing; a foreign inspection team coming onto Cuban soil is another. Write that we are opposed in principle, but don’t shut the door completely. U Thant arrives in two days.

I will instruct the Cuban batteries not to open fire, but only for as long as the negotiations last, and without revoking the declaration published yesterday concerning our decision to defend our airspace. I must also inform you that we are opposed in principle to an inspection of our territory.

choices.text: Accept UN verification on the ground along with the cease-fire. If Cuba blocks the verification the Soviet Union promised the UN, Cuba becomes the country that broke the agreement
choices.why: A few inspectors weigh less than being named the country that broke the deal
choices.after: Your reply relieved Moscow and shook Havana. U Thant came on the 30th, and this time his briefcase held a list of military technicians from neutral countries.

choices.text: Order a cease-fire only for as long as the negotiations last, without withdrawing the declaration on defending Cuban airspace, and oppose inspection in principle
choices.why: Put a time limit on the concession and leave a door open on the principle: that is the ground to negotiate on
choices.after: Your reply went out that night. The batteries were ordered to hold fire, but on the 29th the American low-level planes came back, and a belated report came up that one battery had opened fire. In New York the Soviets proposed that the Red Cross inspect ships bound for Cuba, and on the 30th U Thant boarded his plane for Havana. In 1992 you will put it this way: the Soviet government asked us to stop firing, and yes, but only while the negotiations lasted, only while the negotiations lasted.

choices.text: Refuse the cease-fire. Yesterday’s declaration on defending Cuban airspace stands, and Khrushchev’s deal does not cover Cuba’s skies
choices.why: If the negotiations belong to the Soviets, the airspace belongs to Cuba
choices.after: Your reply was short, and Alekseev, delivering it, lost his temper with you for the first time. On the morning of the 29th the American low-level reconnaissance planes came again.

note.text: Khrushchev’s letter of 28 October exists in two English translations: the National Security Archive’s reads “patience, firmness and even more firmness,” the Wilson Center’s “patience, self-control and more self-control.” The three translations of Castro’s reply also differ slightly (opposing inspection “in principle,” “in general,” “as a matter of principle”); the text here follows the National Security Archive translation. Gromyko’s instruction to Zorin to answer positively on U Thant’s visit and on access to the launchers was sent the same day. American low-level reconnaissance was suspended for one day on the 28th and resumed on the 29th, and American records state that one of those planes drew fire from the Cuban side.
note.src: NSA 19621028khrlet; WC/UMD 114504; NSA 19621028caslet; WC/UMD 114503; PBS jfk-airspace; WC/UMD 111800; FRUS XI d103; FRUS XI d113

FC-11.unknown: In New York U Thant was writing to the three governments to confirm the terms of the agreement. Through Gromyko, Moscow had instructed Zorin to answer positively on U Thant’s visit and on access to the launchers, without asking Cuba. In Washington the Joint Chiefs read Khrushchev’s broadcast as a ploy to gain time and urged that the Monday air strike be kept ready, and Kennedy called off that day’s low-level flights. The United States recorded that one of the planes back over Cuba on the 29th drew fire from the Cuban side.

FC-12.time: 3:10 p.m. on 30 October to noon on the 31st, Havana
FC-12.title: Cuba Is Not Austria
FC-12.clock: One day until U Thant leaves (evening of the 31st)

telegram.cls: Personal letter (delivered by Alekseev on the 31st)
telegram.subject: On the letter of 28 October and the conversation with the ambassador
telegram.text: We have received your letter of 28 October and the reports on the talks that you and President Dorticós had with our ambassador. We understand your situation and take into account the difficulties you face. / There are those who say we did not consult enough. We believe we did consult with you: we received your cables, each more alarming than the last, and finally your cable of 27 October saying an attack was imminent within 24 to 72 hours. / We consider the proposal in your cable of 27 October incorrect, although we understand your motivation. It would have been not a simple strike but the start of a thermonuclear world war. / Shooting down the American plane over Cuba proved useful in the end, because it ended without complications. Let it be a lesson for the imperialists. / We obtained from the United States a commitment not to invade Cuba and not to permit its Latin American allies to do so. We achieved this without a nuclear war.

FC-12.event: At 1:15 p.m. on 30 October U Thant landed in Havana aboard a chartered plane of the Brazilian airline Varig, accompanied by Loutfi, Tavares de Sá and Brigadier Rikhye. The United States has announced that it will suspend the quarantine and reconnaissance for the two days of his visit. At launch sites across the island Soviet troops are already taking the missiles down. Roa reports from New York that Kuznetsov, sent from Moscow, is talking about Red Cross inspection of ships.
FC-12.scene: At 3:10 p.m. the first talks began at the Presidential Palace. U Thant passed on three American proposals: verification on the ground by a UN team; UN reconnaissance aircraft; or reconnaissance planes with Cuban, Soviet and American crews aboard together, for two to three weeks. And a promise that the United States would publicly pledge not to invade and would lift the blockade. You asked where the United States got the right to demand this: was it a right, or a demand resting on force? Cuba is not Austria, nor the Sudetenland of Czechoslovakia, nor the Congo. Conditions that can be imposed only on a conquered country are unacceptable; to impose them, they would first have to destroy and annihilate Cuba. Why should a withdrawal the Soviet Union had publicly promised the UN need the further guarantee of an inspection of Cuba? Dorticós asked where the danger of war lay: in the weapons Cuba had, or in America’s aggressive intentions? The second session, on the morning of the 31st, was closed, and it agreed on the return of Major Anderson’s body. U Thant said he would like to leave two or three UN staff in Havana. And that day Alekseev arrived with Khrushchev’s letter of 30 October. Twice as you read it, you broke off.

voices.text: Where does the danger of war lie? In these or those weapons that Cuba has, or in the aggressive intentions of the United States toward Cuba? Why should inspection, the acceptance of inspection, be the condition for guaranteeing peace?

voices.who: Fidel Castro (transcript of the talks of 30 October)
voices.text: Cuba is not Austria, nor the Sudetenland of Czechoslovakia, nor the Congo. Cuba is most firmly resolved to defend its rights. We cannot accept conditions that could be imposed only on a conquered country. They would first have to destroy and annihilate Cuba, and in any case they will find no one here to accept humiliating conditions.

voices.who: Aleksandr Alekseev (Castro’s words as reported in his cable of 31 October)
voices.text: It is not some Cuban comrades but the whole Cuban people who do not understand the decision to withdraw the special weapons. In the cable of the 27th I did not propose striking the enemy’s territory first during the crisis. I was speaking of the case of aggression against Cuba, in which Soviet people would be dying together with Cubans.

Comrade Prime Minister, close the door to U Thant, but keep the door in New York open. Lechuga and I will meet Kuznetsov and Stevenson. The five points must go on the agenda in New York, not in Havana.

choices.text: Reject one-sided inspection in any form and put the five points on the agenda. Agree only to return Major Anderson’s body, and pass everything else to New York
choices.why: The missiles may leave, but sovereignty is not up for negotiation
choices.after: U Thant left Havana on the evening of the 31st and, landing at Idlewild in New York, said the dismantling was under way and would be finished by Friday. On 2 November Mikoyan landed in Havana, and he stayed until 26 November. On 20 November Kennedy announced the lifting of the blockade, and that day Soviet forces were ordered to load the tactical nuclear warheads in Cuba onto ships and send them home.

choices.text: Accept Red Cross inspection of Soviet ships alone, in Cuban ports, and refuse verification of Cuban airspace and territory
choices.why: The ships are Soviet, so inspecting them does not touch Cuban sovereignty
choices.after: In New York the Soviets pressed for Red Cross inspection at sea, and the Americans said inspection in Cuban ports would be easier. On 8 November the Red Cross withdrew, saying its statutes did not permit it, and in the end the US Navy checked the departing missiles by eye at sea. No one set foot on Cuban soil. On 20 November the blockade was lifted.

choices.text: As U Thant asks, accept two or three UN staff staying on and verification by neutral technicians, for the period of the negotiations only
choices.why: With the UN in Havana, the other side becomes New York, not Washington
choices.after: Before leaving, U Thant told Brigadier Rikhye to stay on in Havana. Two UN staff unpacked at a hotel, and in New York lists of neutral countries began to circulate.

note.text: The transcript of the first session on 30 October was made public when Castro read it out on CMQ television on 2 November (a transcript released by the Cuban side; FBIS translation). The second session on the 31st has remained closed, and the only UN record is its press releases. Alekseev delivered Khrushchev’s letter of 30 October on the 31st, and Castro’s two reactions are in Alekseev’s cable of the 31st. In his notes before dictating the letter, Khrushchev wrote of Castro “an astonishing man” and “out of despair,” and he told Novotný of Czechoslovakia that he had been “absolutely stunned.” Castro’s reply of 31 October (read from a scan) rebutted the claim that there had been consultation and explained once more that he had meant not that the Soviet Union should strike first during the crisis, but that it should act without wavering if an invasion came. The aircraft and the members of U Thant’s party are as given in UN press release SG/1364.
note.src: CMQ 1962-11-02; PBS jfk-defendcuba; WC/UMD 112640; WC/UMD 300937; WC/UMD 115219; WC/UMD 115474; SG/1364; SG/1368; NSA 621031

pressure.title: Only on a Conquered Country
pressure.text: All three proposals U Thant brought would have foreigners looking at Cuban soil or Cuban skies, and since the night of 22 October you have said you will not accept UN observers. To you inspection means recognizing an American right to decide what weapons Cuba may have, and on 28 October you already wrote to Khrushchev that you oppose inspection in principle. In the second session you agreed to return Major Anderson’s body, and U Thant asks you to cut the passage rejecting inspection from your speech of 1 November. Khrushchev’s letter of 30 October, which Alekseev brings that day, says your cable of 27 October proposed a Soviet nuclear first strike and that the proposal was mistaken, and adds that the shootdown was useful in the end. You answer that it is not some comrades but the whole Cuban people who do not understand the withdrawal of the special weapons, and say that either the translation was wrong or Khrushchev misunderstood. Hearing of the deal on the radio on 28 October is still a humiliation.
pressure.src: CMQ 1962-11-02; WC/UMD 115474; WC/UMD 112640; PBS jfk-defendcuba; NSA 19621028caslet; SG/1368; Castro 1992 [secondary]; NSA 621031

FC-12.unknown: That day the Yugoslav ambassador in Havana wrote home that Fidel had been very stubborn and had accepted nothing. Before dictating his letter of 30 October, Khrushchev noted that you were “an amazing man” and that your proposal had come “out of despair,” and the same day he told Novotný of Czechoslovakia that reading your letter had left him “utterly appalled.”

FC-H1.title: The Law on Our Side
FC-H1.event: On 4 September Kennedy issued a statement that if ground-to-ground missiles or other offensive weapons were introduced into Cuba, the gravest issues would arise. Che came back with word that Khrushchev was putting off the signing and would announce the agreement himself when he came to Havana in November. To the suggestion that Cuba announce it on its own, there was no answer.
FC-H1.scene: The text of the agreement stands just as Cuba drafted it, and it names no types of weapons.
