The Soviet Union will send forces to Cuba; the arms of service and the areas where they are stationed are to be settled by the representatives. If you print this document on the front page of Revolución, Cuba becomes a sovereign state that has published a treaty concluded with its ally, and on the day the missiles are discovered, they will be the consequence of a treaty. But if Cuba reveals what Khrushchev wants hidden, Moscow may read it as betrayal, and Washington may read publication of the treaty as disclosure of the missiles. The first ship carrying missiles has already put in at Mariel.

voices.text: He said November. By November the missiles will all be standing, and announcing it then makes it a fait accompli. That is his calculation. If Cuba announces first, it wrecks that calculation, and he is not a man who forgets such things.

If we publish only the agreement and say nothing about the weapons, Cuba’s hands are clean at the UN. If the Americans come out with the missiles, we answer with the agreement. But a treaty published without Soviet consent is one the Soviets could disown.
Fidel, if you publish it, Moscow won’t be able to trust you. An alliance that has to guard your mouth instead of the missiles won’t last long. Just hold on until November.

choices.text: Announce the conclusion of the agreement and its articles, without the types of weapons. Even without Soviet consent, a treaty covering Cuban territory is Cuba’s to make public
choices.why: Better a declaration before you are found out than excuses after
choices.after: Revolución printed the full text of the agreement. Moscow kept silent for three days, and on 11 September a TASS statement repeated word for word that the arms sent to Cuba were purely defensive. Washington answered with a statement on 13 September, and the reconnaissance flights increased. The treaty was public, but the photographs Kennedy produced on 22 October were bigger than the treaty.

choices.text: Drop the announcement and accept Khrushchev’s November timetable. Until then the Cuban government will neither deny nor confirm the types of weapons
choices.why: An ally that upsets its patron’s calculations is left out of the next ones
choices.after: The agreement remained unsigned. The TASS statement came out on 11 September, and you did not put your name to it. Only when you heard Kennedy’s speech on 22 October did you learn that the Americans had been holding photographs of San Cristóbal for some time.

note.text: This scene is hypothetical. Castro’s 1992 recollections confirm that he wanted the agreement signed and announced openly and that Khrushchev insisted on secrecy, but there is no confirmation that Cuba actually considered announcing it on its own. That Khrushchev meant to sign and announce it during a visit to Havana in November comes from the scholarly literature. Kennedy’s statements of 4 and 13 September and the TASS statement of 11 September are confirmed from the original texts the United States quoted in its letter to the Security Council, S/5181.

FC-H1.unknown: Afterward the American reconnaissance flights continued, and on 14 October a U-2 photographed the launch site at San Cristóbal. The United States then spent six days in White House meetings weighing an air strike against a blockade.

FC-H2.place: Outside Havana, Soviet forces headquarters (El Chico)
FC-H2.title: Two Armies
FC-H2.clock: About 10 hours until the quarantine line takes effect (9 a.m. on the 24th, Havana time)
FC-H2.event: The defense minister’s Order No. 4/389, which Pliyev has brought, told him to raise combat readiness and, if American forces landed, to repel them jointly with the Cuban army. He read that far and no further, and did not say whether the order says anything about the missile division or other units. Joint action to repel, yes; joint command, no.
FC-H2.scene: General Pliyev has come in person. He says he passed your proposal on to Moscow, and that the answer is already in the order he has brought with him. Two armies, two commands. Placing Cuban units in the Soviet order of battle is not in the agreement, and a command that decides air-defense fire jointly does not square with the principle that Soviet forces fire on Moscow’s orders. Soldier that he is, he is sparing with words and begins with the order’s number and the hour it was received. You said that every gun fired on this island must carry Cuba’s say; he said that giving Cuba a say over Soviet weapons is not his to decide. Alekseev sits between you. You must decide whether to press your demand or drop it.

voices.text: Comrade Prime Minister, Order 4/389, sent at 23:30 Moscow time on the 22nd, orders joint repulse; it does not order joint command. This headquarters cannot create what is not in its orders. I have reported the Cuban army’s demand. Moscow will give the answer.

voices.who: Raúl Castro (minister of the Revolutionary Armed Forces)
voices.text: If they say no, the Cuban army will act on its own. The batteries are Cuban batteries, and the Commander in Chief gives the orders. No joint command also means Cuba doesn’t need Soviet permission.
Fidel, if you put the demand to Moscow directly by cable, an answer will come. But if that answer is no, you will have to accept it. Better not to make a demand whose refusal you can’t accept.

choices.text: Drop the demand and cover the Soviet positions with Cuban batteries alone. Without a joint command, Cuba decides when Cuban batteries fire
choices.why: Where you have been refused, what you can gain is a free hand
choices.after: Pliyev nodded, and that nod became the grounds on which, three days later, the Cuban batteries received the order to fire without Soviet permission. The night was far gone, and you had to go to the television studio.

choices.text: Demand a joint command from Moscow directly by cable, and hold the Cuban batteries back from covering the Soviet positions until the answer comes
choices.why: The side that lends its strength can set the terms
choices.after: The cable went out, and the answer came on the 25th: the two commands would remain separate, as the agreement provided. For those two days American planes flew over the Soviet positions at 100 meters, and Alekseev said he would report to Moscow that Cuban cooperation had been withheld. You had to go to the television studio.

note.text: This scene is hypothetical. Alekseev’s original cable records that on 23 October Castro raised the idea of placing Cuban units in the Soviet order of battle as divisions, but there is no record of a formal demand for a joint command. The content of Order No. 4/389 (joint repulse, excluding the missile and nuclear warhead means) and the time it was received come from the original Soviet military documents.

FC-H2.unknown: Order No. 4/389 had gone out at 11:30 p.m. Moscow time on the 22nd, and its last line excluded all the means of the missile division and the nuclear warhead units. Even if a landing came, the Soviets were to fight with conventional weapons only.

FC-H3.title: The Word “Defensive”
FC-H3.clock: About 5 hours until the quarantine line takes effect (9 a.m.)
FC-H3.event: On television you said that Soviet strategic rockets are in Cuba. You said they were the result of an agreement a sovereign state had concluded with its ally, and that Cuba has the right to possess any weapons it chooses. Moscow’s statement of the 23rd called those weapons “exclusively defensive in purpose,” and in his speech on the 22nd Kennedy said Gromyko had told him the same thing at the White House the Thursday before.
FC-H3.scene: When you came out of the studio, Alekseev was waiting. He was not angry. He said only that Moscow would read this speech in the morning, and that Washington would be the first to notice that the Soviet statement and the Cuban prime minister’s words did not match. In his speech on the night of the 22nd Kennedy said the Soviets had lied, and you have in effect confirmed it. But for the first time the Cuban people have heard from their prime minister’s own mouth what is on their island, and in the streets they speak with pride of his not hiding it. A cable will come from Moscow in the morning. Before then you must decide what to say next.

voices.text: Fidel, Moscow is still saying defensive. You said strategic rockets, so now one of you has told a lie. Washington will pin it on the Soviet side. Can you set it right in your next speech?

voices.who: Che Guevara (by telephone from Pinar del Río)
voices.text: Well done. The Soviet soldiers by the launch sites heard it on the radio. They were the first to be glad that what they had been hiding no longer has to be hidden. Whatever Moscow says, what is here is here.

In New York last night, García-Incháustegui held the line of neither denying nor confirming. Now that the Prime Minister has confirmed it, the delegation cannot go back to that line. If we are not going back, then demand that the Soviets publish the agreement. Weapons we have acknowledged need a law behind them.

choices.text: Bow to Moscow’s wishes: in your next speech, walk it back by calling the weapons defensive, and do not mention their type again
choices.why: Words left at odds with your patron’s statement will hurt you both the longer they stand
choices.after: The next day you called the weapons defensive several times and never said the word rockets. The people of Havana noticed the difference, and Washington read the two speeches side by side.

choices.text: Hold to the public line, and demand that the Soviets publish the military agreement of May, late as it is. Weapons you have acknowledged need a law behind them
choices.why: Take back what you have said once, and no one will believe the next thing you say
choices.after: No answer came from Moscow. From then on Soviet statements avoided the word “defensive,” though they did not deny the missiles either. At the UN on the 25th Ambassador Zorin had no answer to Stevenson’s photographs, and word came from the delegation in New York that the Havana speech had made things harder for him.

note.text: This scene is hypothetical. In his actual speech of 23 October Castro neither denied nor confirmed the presence of missiles (report of the Dutch ambassador, Boissevain), and in 1992 he recalled that Cuba never joined the “game” of denying the nature of the weapons. The Soviet phrase “exclusively defensive in purpose” is in the original text of Khrushchev’s letter of 23 October to Kennedy.

FC-H3.unknown: In Moscow, on the 23rd, the Presidium had already ordered the ships outside the blockade line to turn back, a decision that appeared in no statement.

FC-H4.time: 1 November to mid-November, Havana and New York
FC-H4.place: Havana, the Presidential Palace / New York, UN Headquarters
FC-H4.title: The Word “Verification”
FC-H4.event: According to Roa in New York, U Thant returned there on 1 November, met Mikoyan, and reported that Cuba had accepted, for the period of the negotiations only, UN staff staying on and verification by neutral technicians. The Soviet side welcomed it; the American side asked separately, Roa says, whether the photographs from its own reconnaissance planes could be replaced by UN verification. Two UN staff are at a Havana hotel, and in New York Brazil has put forward a plan for inspection by a group of neutral ambassadors, and U Thant a plan for a mobile verification team of neutral personnel.
FC-H4.scene: Verification is inspection that avoids the word inspection. But the moment Cuba accepted the word, its counterpart became the UN rather than the United States, and the blockade, halted during U Thant’s visit, never resumed. No American low-level planes came while the UN team checked the launch sites, and the Soviets did not hurry the dismantling. The five points reached the agenda through the mouths of neutral ambassadors. Mikoyan came to Havana and stayed three weeks, and his talks with you dragged on over the powers and the term of the verification team, not the missiles. The ending is decided here.

voices.who: Raúl Roa (foreign minister, by telephone from New York)
voices.text: Comrade Prime Minister, Stevenson says no reconnaissance planes will fly while the UN verification team is there. If the missiles are gone by mid-November, the blockade simply ends. Brazil and Mexico say they will put the five points on the agenda. The two UN staff in Havana are the guarantee of all of it.

voices.who: Raúl Castro (minister of the Revolutionary Armed Forces)
voices.text: UN staff looking at the launch sites, we can stand. Looking at Cuban batteries, no. Get a clause that confines the team’s powers to Soviet weapons. Without it, the next step is inspection of the Cuban army.

choices.text: Accept UN verification through to the end, on condition of a clause confining the team’s powers to Soviet weapons and launch sites
choices.why: The UN’s eyes are less humiliating for Cuba than American photographs
choices.after: The verification team stayed in Havana until December. The missiles were loaded onto ships before the eyes of UN staff, and the blockade was never proclaimed again. Of the five points, the end to violations of Cuban airspace was achieved in practice, and Guantánamo went onto the agenda and came off it again.

choices.text: Give notice that the UN staff’s stay will end if the team tries to inspect Cuban military installations, and fall back on Red Cross inspection in port
choices.why: Not even the UN gets to see Cuban weapons on Cuban soil
choices.after: The UN staff saw only the Soviet launch sites and left at the end of November. The United States accepted their report but added a procedure for checking the missiles by eye at sea, and the blockade ended without any formal proclamation.

note.text: This scene is hypothetical. In fact Castro turned down the request for UN staff to stay on on 31 October, and in his letter to U Thant of 15 November he again stated his refusal of one-sided inspection. But the request for UN staff to stay, Brazil’s plan for inspection by a group of neutral ambassadors (6 November), U Thant’s idea of a mobile verification team (17 November) and the term “verification, not inspection” (12 November) were all proposals actually put forward.

FC-H4.unknown: In those weeks Washington put up with Soviet missiles remaining in Cuba a few weeks longer under UN verification, and suspended its low-level flights while the UN team checked the launch sites.

FC-H5.place: Havana, residence of the Soviet ambassador, Alekseev
FC-H5.title: Luna
FC-H5.clock: About 3 hours until the American morning reconnaissance
FC-H5.event: Besides the missile division, the Soviet forces in Cuba have tactical weapons. All you know is that the Lunas are among them; how many warheads there are, and who has the authority to use them, the Soviets have not said.
FC-H5.scene: One more paragraph has gone into the letter. It asks that, because an American landing force on the beaches would be too large to stop with conventional weapons, the commander of Soviet forces in Cuba be given the authority to use tactical nuclear weapons without waiting for orders from Moscow. Alekseev, taking it down, stopped writing. He will have to report that the Cuban prime minister knows these weapons exist, and he will have to report the request itself. He did not say how Moscow would read it. He asked only one thing back: do you know they would go off on Cuban soil? You said you did. The letter is not yet sealed.

voices.text: Fidel, if those weapons are used, the landing beaches disappear. Cuba’s beaches. You know and I know what America would answer with after that. Put this paragraph in and Moscow will come to fear you. I will pass it on. But Moscow will also learn that you know about this.

If those weapons are used while the landing force is on the beaches, the Cuban army will be there too. In 1961 we finished it in 72 hours. The enemy is different this time, but so is the Cuban army. Put it in the letter as well that we can fight without those weapons.

choices.text: Send the letter with the request as it stands. A weapon on the island that could stop a landing is as good as none if it cannot be used
choices.why: Deterrence deters only if the other side knows it can be used
choices.after: The letter went to Moscow that morning. No answer came from Moscow on that paragraph, and Pliyev said not a word about the nuclear means. Three hours later, something fell from the sky over Banes.

choices.text: Strike out the paragraph and keep only your views on what the Soviet Union should do in case of invasion. Do not name the weapons
choices.why: A document that names the weapons never comes back
choices.after: The paragraph was struck out, and the letter went to Moscow that morning. Four days later, from Khrushchev’s reply, you would learn that he had read the remaining sentences as a proposal that the Soviet Union strike first with nuclear weapons. Three hours later, something fell from the sky over Banes.

note.text: This scene is hypothetical. Castro’s letter of 26 October contains no request for delegated authority over tactical nuclear weapons. But the number of tactical nuclear warheads in Cuba (Luna 12, FKR 80, Il-28 bombs 6) is confirmed by the withdrawal order of 20 November and Savranskaya’s count, and the unsigned draft of 8 September, the exclusion of nuclear means in the order of 22 October and the reaffirmed ban in cable No. 76639 of 27 October are confirmed by the original Soviet military documents. Castro is reported to have told Lechuga in November that there were tactical nuclear weapons in Cuba and that Cuba should keep them (secondary).
note.src: WC/UMD 117316; WC/UMD 117337; Malinovsky 9/8 draft; Savranskaya 2012 [secondary]; Stage 1 issue 1

FC-H5.unknown: The Soviet forces in Cuba held 12 warheads for the Luna rockets, 80 for the FKR cruise missiles, and 6 nuclear bombs for the Il-28s. On 8 September the Defense Ministry in Moscow had drafted a directive allowing the commander on the spot, if communications were cut and a landing came, to use those weapons on his own judgment, but Malinovsky did not sign it, and Order No. 4/389 of 22 October explicitly excluded the nuclear means. At 4:30 p.m. Moscow time that same day, the defense minister sent Pliyev cable No. 76639, firmly reaffirming the ban on using nuclear weapons.

FC-H6.place: Havana, General Staff of the Revolutionary Armed Forces
FC-H6.title: Monday
FC-H6.clock: A few hours since the first strike; no telling when the second will come
FC-H6.event: On the morning of the 29th six American low-level reconnaissance planes came in again, and the Cuban batteries fired. One was hit and went down in the sea on its way back to Florida. In the afternoon US Navy and Air Force planes struck two Soviet SAM sites in the east and a number of Cuban anti-aircraft positions. Radio Moscow announced the withdrawal yesterday, and the missiles are still at their launch sites.
FC-H6.scene: The first strike is over, and a second will come. There have been casualties at the Soviet positions, and Pliyev returned fire without orders from Moscow, with conventional means only. Alekseev reports that Moscow is furious: the day after it announced the withdrawal, Cuba opened fire and handed the Americans a pretext. Why the strike came today you cannot tell, but the result is before your eyes. The 350,000 militia are at their posts, and Che, in Pinar del Río, has said that if the launch sites are hit he will fight alongside the Soviet troops. You must decide whether to keep firing, or to stop and call in U Thant. Either way, the second strike is coming.

voices.text: The Soviet position at Banes has been hit. The Soviets returned fire and the Cuban batteries fired too. If you tell us to stop, we will stop, but a battery that does not fire when the second strike comes is no battery. If a landing follows, we fight on the beaches.

Fidel, Moscow promised the world a withdrawal, and the very next day you shot down a plane. Khrushchev thinks Cuba is trying to drag the Soviet Union into war. Stop firing and send U Thant a cable. That is the only way Moscow stays on your side.

U Thant was due tomorrow. If the strikes go on, he will not come. If we call him in along with a cease-fire, the Americans cannot drop bombs while the Secretary-General is in Havana. That is the last shield Cuba has.

choices.text: Declare an immediate cease-fire and send U Thant an urgent cable asking him to come to Havana. Lay the blame for the strikes on the United States
choices.why: What can stop the second strike is not the batteries but the Secretary-General
choices.after: U Thant came on the 31st, and the second strike did not come while he was in Havana. But Washington kept up the blockade until every launch site was empty, and the invasion force stayed in Florida until December.

choices.text: Go to full-scale combat. Order every battery to fire, demand a joint response from the Soviet forces, and put the militia on the coastal defense line
choices.why: An army that is hit and does not fire back is gone the next day
choices.after: Before dawn on the 30th the second strike hit the launch sites and airfields. The Soviets returned fire with conventional means, and several missiles burned on their launch sites. Reports came in that in Florida the landing force had begun boarding ships.

FC-H7.place: Outside Havana, Soviet forces headquarters (El Chico)
FC-H7.title: The Beaches
FC-H7.clock: About 6 hours until the expected landing (before dawn on 1 November)
FC-H7.event: After two days of air strikes, the landing fleet that sailed from Florida lies off Cuba’s northwest coast. How large a force it carries, you cannot tell. Moscow is all but silent, and according to Pliyev the last order he has received is No. 76639 of 27 October, a firm reaffirmation of the ban on nuclear weapons. The Luna launchers are within range of the expected landing beaches.
FC-H7.scene: In the headquarters at El Chico are you, Pliyev and Alekseev. Pliyev has ordered that the landing be repelled with conventional means, and said that anything beyond that requires orders from Moscow. Moscow is not answering. Three paths lie before you. Demand that Pliyev use the Lunas and send Moscow a cable with the same demand; demand a full Soviet response, as you argued in your letter of 26 October; or fight on the beaches with conventional weapons as in 1961, and take to the mountains if you are pushed back. In 1961 you reckoned that if American forces came in, you would fight a long war at the cost of hundreds of thousands of lives. Tonight that war may begin.

voices.text: Comrade Prime Minister, No. 76639 is categorical. We will not use the nuclear means. We are ready to repel the landing with conventional means. If Moscow issues a different order, things will be different then. This headquarters is awaiting orders.

voices.who: Che Guevara (by telephone from Pinar del Río)
voices.text: The Western Army is on the coast. If they land, we fight on the beaches, and if we are pushed back, we go to the mountains. That is how we won in 1958. If the Soviet weapons are used, don’t forget there will be Cubans on those beaches too.

Fidel, Moscow has already read what you wrote on the night of the 26th as a proposal for a first strike. Make that demand again tonight and they will be sure that was what you meant then. And there is no one in the Kremlin who will grant it.

choices.text: Demand that Pliyev use the Lunas on the landing beaches, and send Moscow a cable with the same demand. Finish it on the beaches
choices.why: Once the landing force gets off the beaches, the whole island becomes a battlefield
choices.after: Pliyev asked Moscow, and the answer came before dawn. What that answer was, and what happened on the beaches, you will soon learn.

choices.text: Send a cable demanding a full Soviet response, as you argued in your letter of 26 October. The invasion has begun, so the case you spoke of then has come
choices.why: You told them beforehand what the Soviet Union must do on the night Cuba is wiped out
choices.after: The cable went out. How Moscow read it, and what it did, you will soon learn.

choices.text: Fight on the beaches with conventional weapons, and take to the mountains if pushed back. Ask the Soviet forces only to fight alongside you with conventional means
choices.why: On beaches where nuclear weapons go off, the defenders do not survive either
choices.after: The landing began before dawn. The Soviet forces fought alongside you with conventional means, and no nuclear weapons were used. What came after, you will soon learn.

note.text: This scene is hypothetical. There was no invasion. The scale of the American invasion plan (Taylor’s “250,000”) is in the original transcript of the ExComm meeting of 16 October, and cable No. 76639 banning nuclear use (27 October) is in the original Soviet military documents. That Castro envisaged a long guerrilla war had American forces intervened in 1961 comes from his 1992 recollections. The two readings of the letter of 26 October are as in the note to FC-07.

FC-H7.unknown: Washington’s invasion plan assumed 250,000 Americans. It was the figure General Taylor, chairman of the Joint Chiefs, had given Kennedy on 16 October as what an attack on Cuba would take.

epilogues.A: Mikoyan arrived in Havana on 2 November and stayed until the 26th, and on some days you would not see him. On 19 November you wrote to U Thant that the Il-28 bombers were Soviet property and that if the Soviet Union wished to withdraw them you would not object; the next day Kennedy announced the lifting of the blockade. None of the five points was won, but no one set foot on Cuban soil, and America’s pledge not to invade remained unofficial. On 31 January 1963 Khrushchev wrote in a long letter that a rift remained between you and invited you to Moscow, and that spring you spent almost 40 days in the Soviet Union. At about the same time in Moscow, the Presidium was putting on record in its minutes that the Cubans were unreliable allies.
epilogues.B: Cuba after the air strikes and the landings is a country without a record. The makings of that war were the long war you had envisaged in 1961, the 250,000-man invasion plan America prepared in October 1962, and the order of 22 October for the 42,000 Soviet troops to fight alongside you with conventional means. Neither side ever managed to count the dead exactly.
epilogues.C: Only a few people knew how Moscow answered your cable that night. Khrushchev later wrote that the letter had come “from despair.” The scale of the damage survives in the U.S. government’s estimates of the time. You made that demand once, and once was enough.
epilogues.E: For the few weeks the UN verification team stayed in Havana, the blockade was not proclaimed again and no American aircraft flew at 100 meters. The missiles were loaded onto ships before the eyes of UN personnel. The five points reached the agenda through the neutral ambassadors and came off it again with only Guantánamo left. U Thant later wrote that Cuba had been in the room.
epilogues.G: Soviet tactical nuclear weapons were used on the landing beaches. Where Washington and Moscow stopped after that decided the world that followed, and where Cuba stood in between, no one recorded. In November Moscow ordered all the tactical nuclear warheads in Cuba loaded onto ships and sent back, and you asked that those weapons be left behind.

dossier.t: You were born on 13 August 1926 at Birán in Oriente province, and in October 1962 you are 36. Your father, Ángel Castro, had come over from northwestern Spain and built up a sugarcane estate as a landowner; you were educated by the Jesuits at the Colegio de Dolores in Santiago and the Colegio de Belén in Havana, then studied law at the University of Havana. On 26 July 1953 you attacked the Moncada Barracks in Santiago and failed, and at your trial you conducted your own defense. Released from prison on the Isle of Pines, you went to Mexico, landed from the Granma in December 1956, and fought for two years in the Sierra Maestra. After Batista fled in January 1959 you became prime minister in February, and in April 1961 at Playa Girón, on hearing of the landing, you threw in all your forces that same day and finished it within 72 hours. Your speeches run on for hours without a text, and with those close to you, such as Alekseev, you talk freely late into the night. In 1961 you counted 300,000 people who could be armed, and reckoned that if American troops came in you would fight a long war at the cost of hundreds of thousands of lives.

Your brother Raúl Castro, 31, is minister of the Revolutionary Armed Forces; he went to Moscow in July and brought back the draft agreement, and in this crisis he is in charge of Oriente in the east. Che Guevara, the Argentine-born minister of industries, took the final text to Moscow with Aragonés at the end of August, and during the crisis commands Pinar del Río in the west. President Osvaldo Dorticós, a lawyer by training, told the UN General Assembly on 8 October that if the United States guaranteed in word and deed that it would not attack, Cuba would need neither weapons nor an army. Foreign Minister Raúl Roa holds that when Cuba’s very life is at stake, no word should be left unsaid. The Soviet ambassador, Aleksandr Alekseev, in Havana since 1959, was named ambassador in June and presented his credentials in August; he is the man you call on before dawn to take down your letters, and the main channel by which your words reach Moscow. In New York there is Ambassador García-Incháustegui, who spoke in the Security Council of good rockets and bad rockets, and with him Carlos Lechuga.

Your greatest fear is invasion. After Girón you believed Washington would come again, and when Biryuzov asked in May 1962 how an invasion could be prevented, you answered that America must be made to understand that attacking Cuba meant war with the Soviet Union. Your second fear is the Soviet Union. You wanted the agreement signed openly, to put the law on Cuba’s side, but Khrushchev insisted on secrecy, and you believe the secrecy puts Cuba at a disadvantage both politically and practically. The authority to order a launch lies in Moscow, and your deepest fear is that Moscow may decide without consulting Cuba. The third is sovereignty and honor. As head of a sovereign state you will never accept observers sent by America, and you believe Cuba is neither Austria, nor the Sudetenland, nor the Congo. Your hope is that America will give a guarantee in word and deed that it will not attack, that the blockade, subversion, pirate raids and violations of your airspace will end, and that Guantánamo will be returned.

movers.intro: Why Castro accepted the Soviet missiles, what he demanded in his letter on the night of 26 October, and where his fury after 28 October came from are questions that have been rewritten again and again as Cuban, Soviet and American records opened one after another. The main views are these:
views: James Blight and Philip Brenner: drawing on Cuban testimony and the 1992 Havana conference, they argue that for Castro the crisis was not about the missiles but about how it would end, on the assumption that Cuba might be wiped out. They read the letter of 26 October not as a demand for a first strike but as a demand that the Soviet Union not back down if Cuba were attacked, and hold that the way 28 October was handled opened a lasting rift in Cuban–Soviet relations.

Aleksandr Fursenko and Timothy Naftali: drawing on Soviet documents, they argue that the deployment was Khrushchev’s idea and that Castro accepted it out of fear of invasion and a wish for a Soviet guarantee. They see Castro’s letter, which reached Moscow on the morning of 27 October, as one of the things that hastened the decision to withdraw, by giving Khrushchev the sense that events were slipping out of control.

Michael Dobbs: argues that the danger on 27 October came from the field rather than from decisions in Washington and Moscow. Fire from Cuban batteries, the shooting down of the U-2 without Moscow’s permission, and Castro’s judgment that an attack was all but certain came together, and he stresses that Khrushchev was horrified when he received Castro’s letter.

Carlos Lechuga: Cuba’s ambassador to the UN at the time, who left a record from the Cuban side. He holds that the roots of the crisis lay in the American threat of invasion and that Cuba was shut out of the settlement. The five points, he explains, were legitimate demands, and the letter of 26 October was a warning of what an invasion would bring.
movers.note: Sources on Khrushchev’s side read Castro’s letter as a proposal for nuclear war born of despair (the note of 30 October and the conversation with Novotný); Castro himself denied this on 31 October and again in 1992. Both readings rest on the same original letter, and which is right is still disputed.
